Last time we found that there is a largest mass that electron degeneracy
pressure can hold up, and that above it nothing we had met could stop a
collapse. This time we meet the stars that run into that limit. A star born
with more than about $8\,M_\odot$ does not end as a white dwarf. It keeps
fusing, stage after stage, each faster than the last, until its core is iron
and there is nothing left to burn. Then the core collapses in about a second
and the star explodes. **The collapse turns the core into a neutron star, or,
if it is heavy enough, into a black hole**, and the explosion hurls the star's
outer layers into space as a **supernova remnant**.

## How to read this lecture

**The main reading for this lecture is Kutner, Chapter 11, Section 11.1**,
which is in the Canvas Files under *Reading Material*, both as a PDF and as
an accessible Word document. It is short: two
subsections, on the core of a high-mass star and on supernova remnants. These
notes do three jobs. They follow the star's last stages as far as iron, they
draw out what Kutner's section leaves for you to see (why the sequence has to
stop at iron, and how much energy a collapse releases), and they give you
exercises on all of it.

### The readings

One thing to know while you read. **Kutner's dividing line between low-mass
and high-mass stars is about $5\,M_\odot$**; the number astronomers use today,
which these notes use, is about $8\,M_\odot$, as in lecture 12.

## A star that keeps going

The early life of a high-mass star looks like a faster version of what we saw
in lecture 11 and lecture 12. It fuses hydrogen in its core, then in a shell
around the core as the core contracts, then fuses helium in the core as the
outer layers swell into a supergiant. The difference comes at the next step.
**A low-mass star never gets hot enough to fuse carbon.** Carbon nuclei have six
protons each, so they repel each other far more strongly than hydrogen nuclei
do, and fusing them takes a temperature of about 600 million kelvin. In a
low-mass star the core stops contracting first, held up by electron degeneracy
pressure. **In a high-mass star the core is heavier, so it is squeezed harder,
and it gets there.** Carbon fusion starts, and the core holds its size once
more.

Each fuel then runs out in turn, and each time the core contracts, heats up and
lights the next one: carbon, then neon, then oxygen, then silicon. Each stage
burns in a shell around the core, so the star becomes layered like an onion,
with the heaviest ashes at the center. Each stage also lasts much less time
than the one before it.

| fuel | time it lasts, roughly |
|:---|:---|
| hydrogen | 10 million years |
| helium | 1 million years |
| carbon | 1000 years |
| neon | 10 years |
| oxygen | 1 year |
| silicon | 1 day |

: Approximate lifetimes of the fusion stages in a very massive star. The numbers are good to an order of magnitude and vary with the star's mass. {#tbl-stages}

```{python}
#| label: fig-burning
#| fig-cap: "How long each stage of fusion lasts in a very massive star, on a logarithmic scale; the longest and the shortest stage differ by nearly ten orders of magnitude. The final stage, silicon, lasts about a day."
#| fig-alt: "A horizontal bar chart with a logarithmic horizontal axis, time in years, from one thousandth to one billion. Six bars, from top to bottom: hydrogen, 10 million years; helium, 1 million years; carbon, 1000 years; neon, about 10 years; oxygen, about 1 year; silicon, about 1 day. Each bar is shorter than the one above it, and each is labeled at its right end with its duration. The silicon bar is shaded orange and the others blue."
#| fig-height: 3.2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.2))

stages = ["hydrogen", "helium", "carbon", "neon", "oxygen", "silicon"]
years = np.array([1e7, 1e6, 1e3, 10, 1, 1 / 365.25])
labels = ["10 million years", "1 million years", "1000 years",
          "about 10 years", "about 1 year", "about 1 day"]
LEFT = 1e-3
y = np.arange(len(stages))[::-1]
colors = [BLUE] * 5 + [ORANGE]

ax.barh(y, years - LEFT, left=LEFT, color=colors, height=0.62, zorder=3)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(LEFT, 1e9)
ax.set_yticks(y, stages)
for yi, t, lab in zip(y, years, labels):
    ax.annotate(lab, (t, yi), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, 0),
                va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlabel("time (years)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
plt.show()
```

@fig-burning shows how fast the end comes. The star spends nearly all of its
life, and nearly all of its fuel, on hydrogen. The last stage, which builds the
iron core, is over in a day.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-stages}

1. Use @tbl-stages to find how many times longer the hydrogen stage lasts than
   the silicon stage. Then say, in one sentence, why a person watching the star
   would have no warning.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The hydrogen stage lasts 10 million years and the silicon stage about one
   day, so the ratio is $\frac{10^{7}\ \mathrm{yr}}{1\ \mathrm{d}}
   \times \frac{365\ \mathrm{d}}{1\ \mathrm{yr}} \approx 4 \times 10^{9}$. The surface of the star, which is
   all anyone can see, does not know what the core is doing until the very
   end.
   :::

:::

## Why fusion stops at iron

Each stage of fusion in @tbl-stages releases less energy per unit of fuel than the one before,
and then, at iron, the process runs out entirely. The reason is in the
**binding energy** of nuclei. The binding energy of a nucleus is the work it
takes to pull it apart into separate protons and neutrons; the binding energy
per nucleon tells you how tightly the average nucleon is held. Kutner's
Fig 9.3 plots it against the number of nucleons, and it is a curve you can read
the whole story from. It climbs steeply for the lightest nuclei, reaches a peak
near iron-56, and then falls slowly for the heavy ones.

Fusion releases energy when it moves nuclei up that curve, toward tighter
binding. Everything lighter than iron is on the climbing side, so fusing two
light nuclei gives energy back. **Iron-56 sits at the top.** Fusing iron into
something heavier moves it down the curve, so the reaction needs energy put in
rather than giving any out. Splitting iron does the same. Iron is the end of
the line for a star because it is the ash that cannot be burned.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about what happens to the core when its fuel is iron"}
A star's core is held up by pressure, and the pressure is kept up by the heat
that fusion makes. Iron fusion makes no heat; it would use heat up. So once the
core is iron, nothing replaces the energy the star radiates. The core starts to
cool, its thermal pressure falls, and gravity has nothing to oppose it but
degeneracy pressure. That is the question for the next section.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-iron}

1. Fusing hydrogen into helium releases about 0.7% of the rest-mass energy of
   the hydrogen. What is that in MeV per nucleon, given that a proton's rest
   energy is $938\ \mathrm{MeV}$? Reading from Kutner's Fig 9.3, helium-4 has a
   binding energy of about $7.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon and iron-56 about
   $8.8\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon. How much more energy per nucleon could be
   released by taking helium all the way to iron? Express the second as a
   fraction of the first.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   Hydrogen to helium releases $0.007 \times 938\ \mathrm{MeV} \approx
   6.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon. Helium to iron could release
   $8.8 - 7.1 = 1.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon more, which is about a quarter as
   much, and it comes in several steps. So each later fuel has less energy to
   give than hydrogen did, and the star is using it up faster, which fits the
   lifetimes in @tbl-stages.
   :::

2. Fusing two iron-56 nuclei takes energy. So does splitting one. Use Kutner's
   Fig 9.3 to explain why both are true.

:::

## The core collapses

Silicon burning in a shell around the center adds iron to the core, and the
iron core grows. It has no fusion to hold it up, and it is dense enough that
it is held up the way a white dwarf is, by electron degeneracy pressure.
Lecture 12 told us the limit: **an iron core that grows past about
$1.4\,M_\odot$ is more than electron degeneracy pressure can support.**

What happens next goes quickly, and it does not stop where a white dwarf's
collapse would. As the core shrinks, its density rises until the electrons
have so much energy that they can be captured by the protons in the iron
nuclei, turning each pair into a neutron and a neutrino,

$$
\mathrm{e}^{-} + \mathrm{p} \;\to\; \mathrm{n} + \nu_{\mathrm{e}} .
$$ {#eq-capture}

This is **neutronization**, and it speeds the collapse up. Every capture
removes an electron, and the electrons were the source of the pressure. The
neutrinos hardly interact with matter at all, so they leave the core directly,
and they carry energy away with them. Kutner adds that the iron nuclei are also
broken apart, which is another reaction that absorbs energy rather than
releasing it. The core runs away: it has nothing to oppose it, and in about a
second its radius shrinks from thousands of kilometers to tens.

A new pressure stops it. The core is now almost entirely neutrons, and
neutrons obey the exclusion principle just as electrons do. **Neutron
degeneracy pressure** is the same physics as the electron pressure of lecture
12, with neutrons in place of electrons, and it can hold up a core of up to a
few solar masses. The result is a **neutron star**, about 10 to 20 kilometers
across. If the core is heavier than about $3\,M_\odot$, nothing we know of can
hold it, and it becomes a **black hole**.

The core stops suddenly, and the material falling in behind it meets something
hard. Kutner describes the material bouncing back, and the neutrinos pushing on
the dense gas around the core to help drive it outward. **How that works in
detail is not completely understood**, and it is still being worked out with
some of the largest computer simulations ever run. What is certain is the
outcome: most of the star's mass is blown away. This is a **type II
supernova**.

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-collapse}

1. How many electrons must be captured by protons to turn an iron-56 core of
   $1.4\,M_\odot$ into neutrons? Count each nucleon as having the mass of a
   proton, and remember that iron-56 has 26 protons among its 56 nucleons.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   **The question.** How many electron captures, @eq-capture, does it take to
   convert every proton in a $1.4\,M_\odot$ iron-56 core into a neutron?

   Each capture uses up one proton, so the number of captures is the number of
   protons. The number of nucleons is the core's mass divided by the mass of one
   nucleon, and $26/56$ of the nucleons are protons. Substitute, with the units
   attached and no arithmetic yet:

   $$
   N_{\mathrm{p}}
     = \frac{26}{56}
       \times \frac{1.4\,M_\odot}{1.6726 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}}
       \times \frac{1.9891 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}{1\,M_\odot} .
   $$

   Now cancel the units, still touching no numbers: the solar masses cancel,
   leaving grams over grams, which cancel too. What is left has no units at all.
   *Do the units make sense?* We were counting particles, and a count is a pure
   number, so yes. Only now the arithmetic:

   $$
   N_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{26}{56} \times 1.665 \times 10^{57}
     = 7.7 \times 10^{56} .
   $$

   About $8 \times 10^{56}$ electrons have to be captured, so about $8 \times
   10^{56}$ neutrinos are made this way. It is a rough count: a real core is not
   pure iron-56, and not every proton is converted. But the number of
   neutrinos is of order $10^{56}$ to $10^{57}$, and it explains why the
   neutrinos can carry away so much.
   :::

2. The core of a high-mass star near the Chandrasekhar mass is roughly the size
   of a $1.4\,M_\odot$ white dwarf, about $1{,}800\ \mathrm{km}$. It collapses to
   a neutron star of radius $12\ \mathrm{km}$ in about one second. What is the
   average speed of the edge of the core during the collapse, and what fraction
   of the speed of light is that? Is the actual speed at the end larger or
   smaller than the average?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The edge falls $1{,}800 - 12 = 1{,}788\ \mathrm{km}$ in about one second, an
   average of about $1{,}800\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, or about 0.6% of the speed
   of light. A collapse speeds up as it goes, because gravity gets stronger as
   the core shrinks, so the speed near the end is much larger than the average.
   :::

:::

## What we see: supernovae and their remnants

A type II supernova is bright. Kutner's Fig 11.1 shows one in a distant galaxy
that is almost as bright as the whole galaxy, and @fig-sn2004dj and
@fig-sn2023ixf show two more: a place in a galaxy before a massive star
explodes there, and the same place after. After a rapid brightening, a
supernova fades over a few months.

Yet the light is a very small part of the explosion.
About 1% of the energy becomes the kinetic energy of the shell of ejected
material and about 0.1% becomes light. **Nearly all of the rest escapes as
neutrinos**, which is why it matters that the star we are describing, unlike
the Sun, makes them in such numbers.

We have caught this once. On 23 February 1987 a star exploded in the Large
Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy next to ours, 168,000 light-years away.
Detectors in a mine in Ohio and in another in Japan recorded about twenty
neutrinos in just over ten seconds, **hours before the light of the explosion
was first seen** [@hirata1987; @bionta1987]. It is the one direct observation
we have of a core collapsing, and of the neutrino burst we just described.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
[The Ohio detector normally recorded about two neutrino events a day, from
cosmic rays striking the atmosphere [@bionta1987]. In the burst it recorded
eight in six seconds, tens of thousands of times its usual rate.]{.aside}
:::

The ejected material is a **supernova remnant**. In a young remnant we can
watch it expand, and in an older one we see a glowing shell, like the Veil
Nebula or Cassiopeia A in Kutner's Fig 11.3. The most-studied remnant is the
Crab Nebula, the debris of a supernova that people saw in the year 1054
(Fig 11.5). Much of its light is **synchrotron radiation**, which Kutner explains in
his Fig 11.4: electrons moving close to the speed of light spiral around
magnetic field lines and radiate as they turn. Synchrotron light is polarized
and has a distinctive spectrum, and the Crab gives it off at every wavelength
from radio to gamma rays. The electrons should lose their energy and fade
within a short time, yet the Crab still shines after a thousand years. **What
keeps it going is a neutron star at its center**, which is the subject of the
next lecture.

Supernova remnants have another job. They throw into space the products of all
the fusion we described above, along with the elements made in the explosion
itself, and mix them into the gas that forms the next generation of stars. This
is why stars that formed recently in the history of our galaxy have more heavy
elements than the oldest ones do. **Much of the oxygen you breathe was made in
stars like this one.**

::: {.callout-warning .textbook-watch title="Textbook watch (Kutner): supernovae are not the only source of the heaviest elements"}
Kutner, and many sources, say that the explosion makes elements much heavier
than iron. Supernovae make a great many elements, at least up to iron. For the
heaviest ones, such as gold, the picture has changed. In 2017 the gravitational-wave detectors caught two neutron stars
merging, the event GW170817 of lecture 10, and the light that followed it
matched what we expect from freshly made heavy elements [@kasen2017]. **How
much of the heaviest material comes from mergers and how much from supernovae
is still being worked out.**
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-remnants}

1. SN 1987A is 168,000 light-years away. When did the star explode? The
   neutrinos reached the detectors hours before the light, though both had
   traveled the same distance. What does that tell you about when each of them
   left the star?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   It exploded 168,000 years before we saw it, because the light took 168,000
   years to arrive. Neutrinos barely interact with matter, so they left the
   collapsing core at once. The light was made by the explosion, which has to
   reach the star's surface before the light can get out, and that takes hours.
   They did not leave at the same time: the neutrinos left hours earlier.
   :::

2. Kutner says about $10^{53}\ \mathrm{erg}$ of energy is released in a type II
   supernova, and about 0.1% of it comes out as light. If that light is emitted
   over 30 days, what is the average luminosity, in solar luminosities? How does
   that compare with a small galaxy of ten billion stars like the Sun?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The light carries $10^{50}\ \mathrm{erg}$, and 30 days is $2.6 \times
   10^{6}\ \mathrm{s}$, so the average luminosity is about
   $3.9 \times 10^{43}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, which is $1.0 \times 10^{10}\,
   L_\odot$ with $L_\odot = 3.83 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. That is
   as bright as ten billion Suns, from a single star, which is why Kutner's
   Fig 11.1 can show a supernova rivaling its whole galaxy.
   :::

3. Stars that formed recently have more heavy elements than stars that formed
   long ago. Explain why, using what a supernova does to the gas around it.

:::

## If you want to go further

None of this section is needed for what comes before or after. It covers what
sits underneath the stages of fusion described above, and Kutner's optional
sections in the readings table go with it.

**Why a high-mass star makes energy faster.** A star like the Sun fuses
hydrogen through the proton–proton chain. In a high-mass star the core is
squeezed to a higher temperature, and hydrogen can fuse through a second route,
the **CNO cycle**, in which hydrogen nuclei fuse onto carbon, nitrogen and
oxygen nuclei that are already there. Carbon is a **catalyst**: it takes part in
the reactions and is returned at the end, so it is not used up. Only a trace is
needed, about 2% of the core's mass, and earlier generations of stars can
make it by the triple-alpha process. The cycle does not release more energy for each
helium nucleus made; it makes them faster, so the star radiates more energy each
second. This is why high-mass stars are so much more luminous than low-mass
ones, and why they live so briefly on the main sequence. Kutner covers the cycle
in §9.3 and Fig 9.6.

**Why the stages take higher and higher temperatures.** Two nuclei fuse only if
they get close enough for the strong nuclear force to take over, and they repel
each other electrically on the way in. A carbon nucleus has six protons and an
oxygen nucleus eight, so the barrier is much higher than for two protons, and
the core has to be much hotter. Kutner makes the estimate for two protons in
§9.2.4. The same argument, with more charge, is why carbon fusion starts at 600
million kelvin and silicon fusion at billions.

**The layered core.** Kutner's Fig 10.3 draws the shells of a high-mass star:
an iron core, with shells of silicon, oxygen, neon, carbon, helium and hydrogen
around it, each burning at the boundary of the shell beneath.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## Summary

| idea | result | why it matters |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Stars above about $8\,M_\odot$ | fuse carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon in turn, each stage shorter than the last | the star ends with an inert iron core, built in the last day |
| Why iron | iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon | fusing or splitting iron takes energy, so fusion cannot hold up the core |
| Core collapse | above $\approx 1.4\,M_\odot$, electrons are captured: $\mathrm{e}^{-} + \mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{n} + \nu_{\mathrm{e}}$ | the collapse runs away until neutron degeneracy stops it, in about a second |
| The outcome | a neutron star, or a black hole above about $3\,M_\odot$ | the second and third compact objects of this course |
| Supernova and remnant | about 1% of the energy to motion, 0.1% to light, the rest to neutrinos | the heavy elements are mixed into the gas that makes new stars |

Every star we have followed so far ended up with a pressure that could hold it
up, even if it took the strange physics of degeneracy. The stars in this lecture
are the first whose cores are beyond the reach of the electrons. Next time we
look at what the collapse leaves behind when it succeeds: the neutron star, and
the pulsars that give it away.
